rv.q: An imaginative though lopsided LCT3 production, which opened Monday, the show finds many instances of humor and insight in a story about a small-town youth group in 1996. New Jersey.

A slow-boil confession that gently but insistently pulls you into the deep end, it left me swimming in a pool of my own ambivalence.
Under the both sneaky and sharp direction of Annie Tippe, Jonas and her five actors turn the play’s plethora of ellipses into a work of sly, dark humor.
Pak, Doman, Fang, and Geevaratne are transcendent as the quirky quartet of adolescent parishioners, each manifesting distinctively awkward cadences and stances across shifting social situations.
Director Annie Tippe and an enthusiastic cast clearly have faith in Jonas’s religious service of a script, making believers out of all of us.

cn.t: Julia May Jonas's inventive religious comedy earns praise for its clever theatrical transformation of the theater into a church setting and its sharp, darkly humorous exploration of faith, sexuality, and youth group dynamics.
